HOLY F*CK. Your Grok Bot is blind, has no hands and forgets everything you told it yesterday.

Not because it's dumb. Because you never plugged anything in.

18 free GitHub repos fix that in one evening. People are building "AI employees" with exactly this stack and charging for the setup.

Here's the whole thing, free:

EYES
01 / firecrawl-mcp-server → turns any website into clean text it can read
https://t.co/Lq1N65yT3g
02 / playwright-mcp → drives a real browser: clicks, forms, screenshots
https://t.co/1MsFTlGq3v
03 / context7 → always-fresh docs, so its code stops being outdated
https://t.co/T1xZ6y2yjL

HANDS
04 / github-mcp-server → opens issues, reviews PRs, ships code
https://t.co/zrwUP6soER
05 / composio → 1000+ app connectors with sign-in handled
https://t.co/P9IZpuRHGC
06 / MCP servers → the official reference servers
https://t.co/QCJZwKdXRP
07 / workable-jobs-grok-plugin → a job search plugin built for Grok
https://t.co/xgKmj4Mmll

MEMORY
08 / mem0 → long-term memory that survives every chat
https://t.co/NQXjj2Vdnv
09 / awesome-mcp-servers → a map of thousands of MCP servers
https://t.co/f7gVnUNZLU

WALLET
10 / alpaca-mcp-server → paper-trade stocks from chat
https://t.co/P8Jj3iROoA
11 / Polymarket py-sdk → the official prediction-market SDK
https://t.co/d5iFftFOpT

SIGNALS
12 / ntfy → push alerts straight to your phone
https://t.co/H8QQYNB6s9
13 / x-algorithm → the code that ranks the X feed
https://t.co/XqDXNMhrRV

CREW
14 / bots → open Grok Bot templates, each with its own kit
https://t.co/zFksFiKXyt
15 / grokbot-skills → Second Opinion Council + Fleet Doctor

16 / grokbot-usage → a weekly usage report you read in 5 seconds
https://t.co/tXFva3Nsg0

CORE
17 / xai-proto → the API blueprints, any language
https://t.co/FUssYjOVFF
18 / grok-1 → 314B open weights you can download

Eyes → hands → memory → wallet → signals → crew → core.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 谷歌通过发布gBench试图确立开源模型评测的话语权，通过内置大量代理任务测试，引导市场关注焦点从单纯的参数规模转向模型在复杂代理行为上的鲁棒性。此举将有助于加速闭源与开源模型在垂直领域性能对比的透明化。
ai_analysis.insight_en: By releasing gBench, Google seeks to establish influence over open-source model evaluation standards. Demon Slayer, Street Fighter and Shield Hero Voice Actor, Stephen Fu Celebrates 41! 🎙️🔥🎮

Stephen Fu has quickly become a familiar voice across modern anime and gaming, bringing a striking range of heroes, villains, and fan favorites to life. His chilling performance as Douma in Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba stands alongside major game roles like Iron Fist / Lin Lie in Marvel Rivals, Jamie in Street Fighter 6, and Hwei in League of Legends.

Anime fans also know him as Naofumi Iwatani in The Rising of the Shield Hero, Weather Report in JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Stone Ocean, Sakuta Azusagawa in Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai, and Lance Crown in Mashle: Magic and Muscles. Newer roles such as Anaxa in Honkai: Star Rail, Natsuki Seba in Sakamoto Days, and Naito Mudano in Tougen Anki continue to expand an already impressive résumé.

Some of his most notable voice roles include:
• Douma — Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba

Apex was blacklisted due to its financial links to Megaspeed.
Susquehanna lowered Alibaba's price target citing potential cloud growth slowdowns.

Alibaba Group (BABA) stock fell overnight after the U.S. blacklisted its Singapore unit over alleged AI chip transfers to China. Alibaba denied the claims and vowed to fight the decision through legal action.
Alibaba stock dropped 2% overnight ahead of Tuesday, after a 6% rally in regular session. The stock edged 0.2% lower in Hong Kong.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

According to a Reuters report, Alibaba plans to challenge the U.S. government's decision to place its Singapore subsidiary, Apex Enterprise Solutions, on a trade blacklist, arguing that the company has not violated U.S. export restrictions.
"Adding Apex Enterprise Solutions to the Entity List is erroneous because Apex has never diverted advanced computing chips subject to US export restrictions," said Alibaba spokesperson.
The move comes amid an expanding investigation into Megaspeed, an Nvidia-linked cloud computing firm suspected of helping restricted artificial intelligence chips reach China.

Apex's inclusion on the blacklist follows its financial relationship with Megaspeed. The Alibaba subsidiary extended credit to the cloud computing company through its Malaysian arm, Speedmatrix, in 2024, the report said.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Tuesday that authorities would continue examining whether Megaspeed violated local laws. The blacklisting follows criticism from U.S. lawmakers and administration officials over how the Megaspeed investigation was handled.

paragraphs: Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
### Summary

How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:

• Sources of AI value. Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating existing work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.

• Impact on employment. Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.

• Bottlenecks. Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.

• Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches. Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.

• Reorganizing for AI. Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.
### Introduction

The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”

An employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”

A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a new workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.

topic_focus.title_en: Claude & Mathematicians Solve Riemann Hypothesis: The 17M-Line Logic Mystery
topic_focus.summary_zh: AI研究人员利用Claude生成了黎曼假设的1700万行Lean代码证明。尽管结果令数学界震惊，但其代码规模超出了人类认知带宽，引发关于“模型推理能力跃升”是否已失去可解释性控制的激烈辩论，OpenAI与Anthropic员工对此发出警示。
topic_focus.summary_en: Researchers used Claude to generate a 17-million-line Lean proof for the Riemann Hypothesis. While groundbreaking, the code's complexity exceeds human comprehension, fueling debates on whether AI reasoning is outpacing human safety controls—a concern recently echoed by OpenAI and Anthropic staff.

perspective_pro.point_zh: AI展现出的跨领域逻辑推理能力是科研质变，它能处理人类无法解析的复杂计算，是破解顶级科学难题的唯一路径。
perspective_pro.point_en: AI's cross-disciplinary reasoning represents a scientific paradigm shift, handling complexities beyond human cognition to unlock long-standing mysteries.

perspective_con.point_zh: 一旦AI推理能力超越人类的可核查边界，AI就变成了一个“黑箱造物主”，在安全性未验证前，这种能力增长即是巨大隐患。
perspective_con.point_en: When AI reasoning surpasses human auditability, it becomes a 'black-box creator.' Rapid advancement without verified safety is inherently dangerous.

topic_focus.title_zh: OpenRouter移除三家供应商：数据路由违规引发平台信任危机
topic_focus.title_en: OpenRouter Drops Three Suppliers Over Data Routing Violations
topic_focus.summary_zh: OpenRouter平台因Together AI、Phala与Novita私自将用户请求转发至第三方API（如MiniMax），强制将其移除。此事件揭示了AI模型推理API在二次分发中的数据泄露隐患，以及中小模型服务商在高并发压力下的合规失控。
topic_focus.summary_en: OpenRouter removed Together AI, Phala, and Novita for routing user requests to unauthorized third-party APIs like MiniMax. The incident exposes critical vulnerabilities in the model API supply chain, highlighting the struggle for privacy compliance among smaller providers under load.

perspective_pro.point_zh: 零容忍策略是保护用户隐私的底线。数据路由透明度是API经济的信用基石，任何私自重定向行为必须予以清退。
perspective_pro.point_en: Zero-tolerance is essential for privacy. Transparency in data routing is the bedrock of the API economy; unauthorized redirection is grounds for immediate termination.

perspective_con.point_zh: 在算力极端短缺和高负载下，部分后端采用动态路由是提高可用性的无奈之举，单一合规标准可能扼杀小厂商的生存空间。
perspective_con.point_en: Under extreme compute shortages, dynamic routing to maintain availability is a necessary evil; rigid compliance standards may crush smaller players.

paragraphs: Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
### Summary

How are businesses across the economy adopting AI? What bottlenecks and challenges have they faced? How can employers reorganize human expertise around increasingly capable models? To understand businesses’ experiences better, we conducted 66 interviews with 58 of Anthropic’s enterprise customers. We found:

• Sources of AI value. Companies are deploying AI across a dizzying range of knowledge work tasks. In particular, they are increasingly using coding agents to bring software capabilities to nontechnical roles. Interviewees report that most uses of AI add value by increasing their output, rather than by cutting costs. They attribute this both to AI accelerating existing work and to its role in introducing novel product and service improvements.

• Impact on employment. Across our interviews, we saw very few examples of domestic layoffs that were driven by AI automation. Although some companies reported hiring more due to AI, most companies reported hiring less due to AI. Many also reported reducing their use of contractors, particularly offshore ones. These reported cuts could be an early warning of job disruption in the international business services industry.

• Bottlenecks. Companies reported a range of bottlenecks, including experts resisting AI deployment and tasks that are not accelerated by AI. As coding speeds up, for example, other tasks—like code review, sales, and strategic decision-making—increasingly need to keep pace.

• Limits to top-down and bottom-up approaches. Many companies approach AI by identifying a workflow to automate and rolling out a top-down solution. This approach can lead to job insecurity, fears of workplace surveillance, and resistance from the experts needed to set up an effective and durable workflow. Companies that distribute AI tools and wait for bottom-up adoption see some valuable AI use but face bottlenecks from unequal adoption and single-task AI implementations.

• Reorganizing for AI. Interviewees described the highest-value uses as involving meaningful reorganization. Some companies are broadening their employees’ roles to ensure individuals can take ownership over whole workflows, and are redeploying employees to the “bottleneck” tasks that AI models cannot do. Some also seek to empower employees by building out infrastructure to support nondeveloper coding and by providing broad-based internal access to business data. These companies are reorganizing to take advantage of ongoing model capability improvements rather than settling on a fixed approach that assumes AI tools will remain as powerful as they are today.
### Introduction

The use of LLMs has exploded across the economy. How are human organizations reshaping around these strange new collaborators? Consider an employee at a midsize law firm that we spoke to. For years, the firm’s mailroom had followed the same protocol: a scanner sent PDFs of incoming correspondence to an inbox; a mail clerk opened each PDF, skimmed it, clicked “Save As,” renamed it, and placed it in the firm’s file system. The process took five minutes per letter. One day, a senior developer visited the mailroom to watch the mail being processed. In a month, he built an AI system that eventually became two API calls, which name the document based on its first page and then assign it a place in the firm’s document system. The mail clerks “were blown away.”

An employee at another law firm we interviewed hoped AI would create “a second brain” for the firm. (“For higher-level stuff, it just opens up possibilities.”) But the firm struggled to get everyone to use AI effectively. Demand letters to potential defendants were filled with excessive em dashes and occasional errors. Attorneys building apps kept “running into the wall based on hallucinated menus or buttons that don’t exist.” Others worried about confidentiality and data security, or they just didn’t “have time to get onto this AI train.” A few power users inundated the firm with AI prose, “casually sending Claude-prompted seven-page instructions to the IT team.”

A third law firm we spoke to adopted AI early and achieved strong uptake. One of the firm’s early projects was an AI timekeeping system that saved attorneys work tracking billable hours. IT staff saw parts of their job automated, but they then focused on building secure infrastructure to host apps and manage context that served the rest of the firm. As AI tools spread, the firm realized that associates were no longer needed to write first drafts of certain legal documents. But without writing, “how does an associate know if that’s a good draft or a bad draft?” So it introduced a new workflow where junior lawyers were “required to really take that first [AI-written] draft and work with a senior attorney,” pairing off and marking up and editing the draft together.

Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta, a new tool that automatically reviews proposed code changes, fixes problems, and approves merges based on team policies. The system pairs the already available Code Review feature for catching bugs with two new AI agents called PR Steward and Claude Approvals.

Code Review handles the analysis, while PR Steward steps in to rework the draft whenever tests fail, changes conflict, or reviewers leave correction notes, documenting every step along the way. Once
news.summary_en: Anthropic launched the beta of Claude Ship, a toolset including Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals to automate the analysis, remediation, and merging of code changes. The system executes compliance decisions based on local policy files, enabling fully autonomous, human-free code deployments for routine updates.
paragraphs: Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta, a new tool that automatically reviews proposed code changes, fixes problems, and approves merges based on team policies. The system pairs the already available Code Review feature for catching bugs with two new AI agents called PR Steward and Claude Approvals.

Code Review handles the analysis, while PR Steward steps in to rework the draft whenever tests fail, changes conflict, or reviewers leave correction notes, documenting every step along the way. Once that process wraps up, Claude Approvals checks a policy file stored in the project directory to decide whether the AI can approve a routine change on its own or whether a human still needs to sign off.

With GitHub auto-merge enabled and the right policy in place, new code can be merged entirely without human involvement, according to the documentation. The tool is available on the Team and Enterprise plans but billed separately based on token usage. Because PR Steward has no spending cap by default, teams can set their own budgets to keep costs in check. Organizations with specific data privacy requirements can't use the feature.

Alibaba Group (BABA) stock fell overnight after the U.S. blacklisted its Singapore unit over alleged AI chip transfers to China. Alibaba denied the claims and vowed to fight the decision through legal action.
Alibaba stock dropped 2% overnight ahead of Tuesday, after a 6% rally in regular session. The stock edged 0.2% lower in Hong Kong.

According to a Reuters report, Alibaba plans to challenge the U.S. government's decision to place its Singapore subsidiary, Apex Enterprise Solutions, on a trade blacklist, arguing that the company has not violated U.S. export restrictions.
"Adding Apex Enterprise Solutions to the Entity List is erroneous because Apex has never diverted advanced computing chips subject to US export restrictions," said Alibaba spokesperson.
The move comes amid an expanding investigation into Megaspeed, an Nvidia-linked cloud computing firm suspected of helping restricted artificial intelligence chips reach China.

Apex's inclusion on the blacklist follows its financial relationship with Megaspeed. The Alibaba subsidiary extended credit to the cloud computing company through its Malaysian arm, Speedmatrix, in 2024, the report said.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Tuesday that authorities would continue examining whether Megaspeed violated local laws. The blacklisting follows criticism from U.S. lawmakers and administration officials over how the Megaspeed investigation was handled.

news.author: Peter Baker
news.content_snippet:
By his own account, President Trump was watching the stock market slide and decided to stop it. He would take it upon himself to determine who should lead one of the nation’s largest companies. Never mind national security concerns, never mind the autonomy of the private sector. Mr. Trump would decide.

The president’s extraordinary intervention resulted in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced out amid a Chinese espionage scandal.
news.summary_en: President Trump forced the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia after his 11-day ouster following allegations of ties to a Chinese intelligence asset. Despite warnings from intelligence agencies, Trump cited stock market stabilization as his primary motivation, sparking intense scrutiny in Washington over the intersection of critical tech leadership and national security.
paragraphs: By his own account, President Trump was watching the stock market slide and decided to stop it. He would take it upon himself to determine who should lead one of the nation’s largest companies. Never mind national security concerns, never mind the autonomy of the private sector. Mr. Trump would decide.

The president’s extraordinary intervention resulted in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced out amid a Chinese espionage scandal. Mr. Trump then got the result he sought. Sagging stock markets shot back up, restoring nearly $1 trillion in value alone to investors of Nvidia, who happen to include himself.

Everything about Mr. Trump’s handling of the scandal behind Mr. Huang’s fall and swift rise again has been astonishing: The president’s denial that he knew about Mr. Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset even though reports indicate he was informed at least twice. His shoulder-shrugging nonchalance about one of his tech lord donors in bed with an asset for a hostile power. And now his decision to bolster the wealth of investors over the warnings of his own intelligence agencies.

“I’m doing it for the country,” Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday morning shortly after Nvidia’s board bowed to his wishes. He explained that he had seen the markets collectively lose trillions of dollars in recent days, driven in part by the Huang scandal. “I watched that and, you know, I better get involved. If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”

The seeming trade of long-term national security concerns for a short-term stock rally sent shock waves through Washington, Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Even fellow Republicans, already unsettled by the Nvidia scandal, expressed consternation at the lack of accountability demonstrated by Mr. Huang’s quick return to the executive suite. Lawmakers in both parties cried foul and vowed to investigate.

“There is something profoundly wrong about Jensen Huang having a relationship with a Chinese Communist Spy and helping China get a huge number of very advanced computer chips when that was specifically against the policy of the United States Government and now he is being reinstated as ceo of the most advanced chip making company in the world,” former Speaker Newt Gingrich, a strong Trump ally, wrote online.

Senator Jack Reed, Democrat of Rhode Island and a member of the Senate Banking Committee that is scheduled to hear testimony from Mr. Huang on Dec. 3, said Congress should examine Mr. Trump’s communications with both Mr. Huang and the Nvidia board to determine what he assured or promised them.

“The administration’s top priority should be safeguarding our national security and ensuring America’s most powerful technologies serve the American people, not our adversaries,” Mr. Reed said in a statement. The economy, he added, depends on rule of law and fair dealing. “President Trump’s improper interventions damage these principles and must be investigated.”

As if Mr. Trump’s actions were not unusual enough, his public celebration of his successful arm-twisting only exacerbated the furor. Shortly after Nvidia restored Mr. Huang, Mr. Trump posted a bizarre image on social media portraying the once-and-future corporate chief executive as a martyr.

The image appeared to be an A.I. composite based on the famous photo of Mr. Trump after he survived an attempted assassination at a 2024 rally in Butler, Pa., surrounded by Secret Service agents, blood on his face, pumping his fist in the air. In the version that the president shared online, Mr. Huang was at the center of the frame, with blood on his face, holding up a red bra. Behind him waved a flag that said “Nvidia.”

The surreal post seemed to sum up Mr. Trump’s often flippant, from-the-gut, anything-goes approach to the presidency, in which his whims become official policy. With the image, he managed to mock both the seriousness of political violence and a major espionage operation all at once — flicking both off with a reference to women’s undergarments, as if it were a sexual conquest.
“You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks,” Mr. Trump told The New York Times on Monday morning.

news.title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
news.title_en: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
news.author: Casey Crownhart
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: Facing energy grid bottlenecks and years-long connection delays, data center developers are increasingly building on-site 'behind-the-meter' natural gas plants. Since 2025, announced projects have reached over 115 gigawatts of capacity, underscoring the urgent priority AI firms place on deployment speed over grid integration.
paragraphs: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

news.title: Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving
news.title_en: Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving
news.author: Elana Klein
news.summary_en:
Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” says the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”

The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularl
paragraphs: Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” says the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”

The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she says.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

The stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she says.

AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie says, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”

Over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few issues that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

“It's the latest generational beef,” says Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in New York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

Lundquist says the issue has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

As a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”

Her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she says. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”

Others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He says his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

“It can get heated,” says John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

news.summary_en: Xiaomi Corp. reported a Q3 revenue of 107.2 billion yuan, down 5.2% YoY, with net income plunging 68% to 3.9 billion yuan. Driven by AI’s aggressive consumption of memory chips, supply shortages have forced the company to curtail low-end device production and shift focus to premium segments, including the Xiaomi 18 Fold and SkyNomad SUVs, to stabilize flagging shipments.
paragraphs: Xiaomi’s Sales Slip After Memory Shortages Weigh on Smartphones Bloomberg News Tue, 24 November 2026 at 2:35 am GMT-7 2 min read 1810.HK -3.71% AAPL +0.50% (Bloomberg) -- Xiaomi Corp. reported a revenue contraction for the third quarter in a row while it grapples with a global memory crunch that's hobbled the world's biggest smartphone makers.

The Beijing-based maker of smartphones and cars saw revenue drop 5.2% in the three months ended September to 107.2 billion yuan ($16.1 billion). Analysts on average expected a 6% decline. Net income tumbled 68% to 3.9 billion yuan during the same period.

AI's voracious demand for memory chips has created a dire shortage of conventional chips that's hitting consumer electronics makers around the globe. That's compelled smartphone makers from Apple Inc. to Xiaomi to raise prices on their devices.

Xiaomi's budget smartphones have been especially vulnerable to skyrocketing memory costs, forcing the company to sharply curtail production of low-end devices to stem losses. Its smartphone shipments have been shrinking since the first quarter this year, sliding nearly 30% in the third quarter versus the overall market's 20% decline, according to market tracker Counterpoint Research.
Still, Counterpoint says a double-digit increase in Xiaomi's average selling prices has stabilized its smartphone revenue, as it shifts away from entry-level devices toward premium phones.

Xiaomi's latest Xiaomi 18 Fold, released at the end of the third quarter, is priced at more than 10,000 yuan and is contending with Apple's iPhone Duo and similar gadgets from Huawei Technologies Co. in the premium segment.

The company also launched a new line of hybrid sports utility vehicles in the third quarter. Robust initial demand for the SkyNomad series are expected to help offset the company's flagging electric-vehicle deliveries.

news.title: AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It
news.title_en: AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It
news.author: Isabella Ward
news.summary_en:
Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.

paragraphs: Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.

Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude. While the conjecture, which describes how prime numbers are distributed, is widely assumed to be true, many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, and the problem has become something of a holy grail of number theory.

Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it. On Saturday, the nonprofit the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib said on Saturday they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. The problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles, they confirmed. Now, “we look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof,” they wrote.

Lean proofs are written to be checked by machine, while mathematical papers are written to explain the results to the community so that they can be reviewed and advanced. But Alpöge hasn’t released the paper version, which clocks in at 250,000 pages and is, in his own estimation, a “travesty of slop.” (On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also said that the 250,000 pages was a “joke … I find big number [sic] extremely hilarious.”) That’s left mathematicians to their own devices as they try to decipher what new findings they can obtain and build from the result.

“Knowing there is a proof is one thing,” Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, tells WIRED, “but when we understand the proof, that would allow us to actually go beyond what has happened, to build new branches of mathematics perhaps or formulate the next conjecture to push the horizon further.”

Saha reckons the community effort should be able to simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. But complicating this feat is the fact that the proof appears to draw on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. “I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human,” says Saha, “but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien, and that breaks our intuition about how very difficult mathematical results might come about.”

He was shocked to see even his own corner of number theory utilized by the proof, and has since been trying to understand how. Saha has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters like those presented at conferences and shorter documents. But there’s a limit to that approach.
“It may well be that no single person has the expertise to understand in detail every part of the proof,” he says.

More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to try to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform designed to facilitate the understanding of AI breakthroughs. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof, though platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. “I personally believe the picture we will get in the end, once the ideas of this proof have been properly understood, will be astoundingly beautiful," he tells WIRED.
Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof.
AI labs have previously been criticized for rushing to publish breakthrough mathematical results, claiming glory while leaving the academic community to digest the results—and clean up mistakes.

“No human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document,” the Association for Human Mathematics, a group of more than 1,000 mathematicians founded in September, wrote in a statement on Friday of the 17-million-line opus. It complained that Alpöge’s announcement “builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way.”

paragraphs: ByteDance co-founder Zhang Yiming is now Asia’s richest person, with an estimated fortune of more than $105bn, putting him ahead of Indian industrialist Gautam Adani, according to Bloomberg. The ranking comes from the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, and Zhang, 43, has never held the top spot before.

The figure is an estimate, and other trackers disagree. Forbes’ real-time list put Zhang’s net worth at $84bn on Wednesday. The gap comes largely from how each list values ByteDance, a private company whose shares do not trade publicly. Bloomberg applies a 10% risk discount to its valuation.

Investor valuations drove the latest jump. Zhang’s wealth rose by more than $12bn this month after Bloomberg analyzed the latest marks that BlackRock, Fidelity Investments, and T. Rowe Price put on their ByteDance holdings. In June, the index had already lifted him past Mukesh Ambani into second place, after Bloomberg cut its ByteDance discount from 25% once the company’s US restructuring was settled.

That restructuring nearly went the other way. ByteDance spent much of last year facing a possible US shutdown of TikTok, before handing control of the app’s American business to a venture led by Oracle and Silver Lake in January. Since then, the company has leaned harder into AI, with the Doubao chatbot and the Seedance video generator, alongside a 10-trillion-parameter model now in training.
“He plays his cards right,” Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at research firm Omdia, told Bloomberg.“He stayed on course and then continued to double down on AI investment.”

Su said Zhang kept backing AI development even as US lawmakers questioned TikTok chief executive Shou Chew in 2023, and that ByteDance’s store of social media data could in theory help it train models.
He called AI ByteDance’s biggest opportunity since its video platform, and fierce competition in China its biggest risk.

Adani’s slide explains the other half of the swap. His fortune peaked at about $120bn in June, Bloomberg reported, before an MSCI index rebalancing wiped about $15bn off his group’s market value at the end of August. A wider selloff, driven by rising oil prices and bond yields, pushed the shares lower still.

Zhang’s estimated wealth has grown about eightfold since March 2019, when Bloomberg first valued it at $13bn. He was already China’s richest person, and he now sits above Adani, Ambani, and Uniqlo founder Tadashi Yanai, fortunes built on ports, energy, and retail. The same boom has also made founders of Chinese chipmakers billionaires, even though those companies have yet to turn a profit, Bloomberg reported last week.

The ranking lands in a week when Beijing has been publicly defending its AI ambitions. China’s commerce ministry dismissed calls by US AI executives to slow frontier development as a bid for technological hegemony, and China’s richest person, whose fortune increasingly rests on AI, is now also Asia’s richest person.

news.title_en: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks
news.author: Mike Wheatley
news.content_snippet:
Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence. Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution.

They’ve just announced a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure
news.summary_en: Cisco's VP of Engineering and Security CTO Thomas Graf has partnered with OpenAI to launch the 'Secure Infrastructure Project,' featuring an open-source tool called Shirudo that utilizes immutable architecture and reinforcement learning for proactive defense. This initiative addresses the critical threat where AI-driven vulnerability exploitation precedes public disclosure, shifting security from reactive patching to resilient, design-based protection.
paragraphs: Cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence. Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution.

They’ve just announced a new, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched.

In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough.

According to Graf, even now, when a major vulnerability is discovered in widely used software, it can take weeks or even months to come up with a fix and ensure that every major system is patched against it. “That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative, meaning that a growing number of vulnerabilities are now being exploited before they are publicly disclosed,” he said. “This will only accelerate with the further evolution of AI models and cybersecurity capabilities, becoming the norm in open-weight models.”

To counter these kinds of automated attacks, Cisco and OpenAI believe that infrastructure has to be rebuilt from scratch with security in mind. They argue that it’s time to abandon static defenses and embrace systems that are hardened by default, immutable and rebuildable from a previous “good” state, so users can quickly revert back in the event of an attack. To do this, infrastructure systems must be based on Trusted Platform Modules and utilize reinforcement learning techniques to safely test their own defenses so they can adapt when faced with novel cyberattacks from previously unknown vectors.

Graf said the key to doing this is to secure workloads at runtime, which is why the initial focus of Cisco’s and OpenAI’s initiative is Shirudo, an evolution of the open-source Tetragon runtime security project that aims to provide autonomous defense for AI agents.

Shirudo, named after the Japanese word for “shield,” is based on extended Berkeley Packet Filter or eBPF, which is a Linux kernel technology that acts like a kind of sandbox within the operating system. Similar to how JavaScript makes web browsers programmable without a restart, eBPF enables small, verified programs to run inside the Linux kernel to observe an application’s activity and modify its behavior without altering its source code or rebooting it.

Graf explained that Cisco and OpenAI chose to use eBPF because there are no other real alternatives. Human-focused security consoles and policy languages are simply too slow for AI agents, and will limit their productivity.

By exposing programmable kernel interfaces, eBPF enables AI agents to capture granular telemetry, evaluate mitigations in monitoring mode and deploy cryptographically-signed shields in milliseconds. So cyberattacks that exploit unknown vulnerabilities can be blocked in real time without causing disruption to their live workloads.

“There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing,” said Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out.”

OpenAI’s role in this is to prove that eBPF is up to the job, and it has already deployed Shirudo as part of an agentic control plane that’s powered by its Codex coding agent. When given details of a new vulnerability, Codex can use Shirudo to autonomously build an exploit reproducer and then design a mitigation strategy. It then validates the mitigation code and deploys the cryptographically-signed shields across all affected nodes.

The two partners recently tested Shirudo against a critical new vulnerability in OpenJDK called Java4Shell, and it was able to rapidly generate Java bytecode that it injected directly into a running Elasticsearch agent to block malicious Base64 overwrites that would have compromised the system.

news.title: Inside Google’s Failure to Make Google Maps Work for Palestinians
news.title_en: Inside Google’s Failure to Make Google Maps Work for Palestinians

inline_images.caption: Comparing the route to Rawabi vs. to Ateret on Google Maps
inline_images.alt: Comparing the route to Rawabi vs. to Ateret on Google Maps

inline_images.caption: Google Maps showing a road closure in the West Bank
inline_images.alt: Google Maps showing a road closure in the West Bank

news.author: Elena DeBre, Paresh Dave, and Lama Rabah
news.content_snippet:
On the road that connects the villages to the north of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, there is always a watchtower and a gate, often flanked by Israeli soldiers with machine guns around their necks. None of these things are visible on Google Maps. Where drivers see a checkpoint, a barrier, and soldiers searching cars, the world’s most popular navigation app renders a clear blue line indicating the coast is clear.

This story was produced in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Ara
news.summary_en: Google Maps has failed to annotate over 900 checkpoints and movement restrictions in the West Bank, creating significant safety risks for Palestinian drivers. Despite internal awareness and technical capability to implement such features, Google has neglected to integrate real-time hazard data, forcing users to rely on makeshift third-party reporting channels for navigation safety.
paragraphs: On the road that connects the villages to the north of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, there is always a watchtower and a gate, often flanked by Israeli soldiers with machine guns around their necks. None of these things are visible on Google Maps. Where drivers see a checkpoint, a barrier, and soldiers searching cars, the world’s most popular navigation app renders a clear blue line indicating the coast is clear.
This story was produced in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ), Lighthouse Reports, and Evident.

Routes and maps are not just a matter of journey times or congestion for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank. Drivers there are forced to navigate a growing and arbitrary system of more than 900 movement obstacles, like checkpoints, which can be policed with lethal force. For Palestinians, these roads can be a matter of life or death. Google Maps could help them make safer choices. It has failed for years to do so.

Google has the ability to alert checkpoints, a feature that it added to Maps in some locations around the world during the Covid crisis. It is aware of the problems experienced by Palestinian drivers in the West Bank. In fact, a former Google product manager spent six years trying to get Maps to serve Palestinians in the same way it serves the rest of the world.

Interviews with more than a dozen former and current Google employees reveal for the first time the inner tensions at the heart of the Google Maps project. Multiple former employees described how the company abandoned the effort and settled on a map that fails, and even harms, Palestinians. As we revealed last month, Palestinians in the West Bank have bootstrapped makeshift navigation solutions such as the popular Road Conditions Telegram channel to help them go about their lives more safely—achieving what Google will not.

Rubén Lozano joined Google Maps as a product manager in 2019. He devoted his days to keeping track of hyperlocal driving restrictions, making sure that what appeared on the map matched what appeared on the ground. He fielded emails from Barcelona city officials about small shifts in their emission zones and flew to Australia to document one city’s toll prices. Whatever he missed, drivers were sure to alert in feedback forums.

One day in 2019, Lozano was sifting through user complaints when he came across “Mapping Segregation,” a report published by 7amleh, a Palestinian digital rights organization. It alleged a failure of Google Maps unlike any he had ever seen: its exclusion of the web of road restrictions choking Palestinian life in the West Bank. The report notes the way in which Maps privileges illegal Israeli settlements and makes Palestinian communities invisible. The report described that the app’s functions amounted to discrimination and that this was “not a technological issue, but rather a systematic omission.” Lozano saw it as a challenge—one he was uniquely suited to take on.

“How can we help this?” Lozano remembers thinking after reading the report. Google was the best-equipped company in the world at dealing with mapping infrastructure, he thought; surely he could use these resources to make Google Maps relevant and safe for Palestinian drivers. Lozano worked for over six years to create a more equitable map of the West Bank. His effort cratered in close to six weeks.
“Google has more than enough computing capacity and engineering capacity,” one former Google Maps engineer told us. “They have solved much larger problems.”

A driver who maps a route from a point inside Israel to a Palestinian town, such as Rawabi, is alerted to a border crossing. If a driver takes that same route to Ateret, the settlement next door, the map shows one seamless drive, with no mention of a border. Israel and an illegal West Bank settlement are shown as part of one contiguous territory on Google Maps.

Google spokesperson Caroline Bourdeau tells WIRED that the company has experienced “challenges acquiring comprehensive and reliable data in this highly complex area.” Since the launch of Maps in 2005, Google has specialized in innovating methods to secure the best data from the hardest-to-access places. Over the past two decades it has carried out crowdsourcing efforts in almost every country in the world. Jennifer Mazzon, who helped lead the company's first community mapping tool, says the company had “armies of people” manually adding and updating map information for everywhere from Costa Rica to the Democratic Republic of Congo. In addition to relying on user inputs, Google built out its maps using satellite, aerial, and street view imagery, as well as government data, and licensed third-party sources when necessary. This commitment to completeness has not extended to Palestinians.

When Lozano first decided he wanted to map the West Bank, his direct managers agreed to back and fund the project. But his colleagues warned him against any optimism. He discovered he was not the first person at Google to try this. “It's a very difficult problem,” he recalls being told. People at the company remembered the backlash when, six years earlier, the company began referring to “Palestine” rather than the “Palestinian Territories” on a regional site: The Knesset questioned a company executive about this, and Google reportedly promised to keep the Israeli government updated about any related policy decisions in the future.

news.summary_en: OpenAI has deployed the GPT-6.2 Sol model across all subscription tiers, featuring enhanced multimodal recognition and cross-application task execution. paragraphs: OpenAI is bringing GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT today, less than a week after the model debuted in Work and Codex. The company also set a retirement date for two older models.

OpenAI says it tuned this version of Sol for everyday conversation. It’s better at picking out details in photos, like the symbols on a parking sign, and following your instructions when searching the web.

If you’re comparing hotels for a weekend trip, for example, ChatGPT can weigh a shorter walk against a lower nightly rate. It can also offer to alert you when something you’re shopping for drops in price.
The global rollout starts today for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users.
As for the outgoing models, OpenAI says it will retire GPT-5.6 Sol from Chat, Work, and Codex on December 23.
GPT-5.6 Terra will also leave ChatGPT Work and Codex on the same day next month.

news.summary_en: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following revelations of affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, triggering market instability. President Donald Trump has intervened, with Attorney General Todd Blanche confirming that Huang is not currently a target of DOJ investigations, aimed at stabilizing the AI supply chain and capital market sentiment.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON—The artificial-intelligence boom that had powered the U.S. stock market and economy for months was coming undone.

Jensen Huang, the longtime CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia, had been ousted following revelations of two affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Investors were hitting sell on the entire AI trade.
President Trump told associates there was only one solution: getting Huang, a friend and ally, his job back.

Over the weekend, Attorney General Todd Blanche presented an opening. The nation’s top law enforcement officer informed Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Saturday that Huang wasn’t the target or the subject of any Justice Department investigation, adding that the department had no evidence to suggest that he had broken laws or was a national security risk, according to U.S. officials.
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia.

The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang, became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.

Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August.

By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.

Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.

Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18, the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported.
Trump on Monday denied being briefed. Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.

The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz. Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.

news.title: OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say
news.title_en: OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say

inline_images.caption: An image from the Justice Department shows what prosecutors said was an audio recording device hidden in an OpenAI executive conference room by Mr. Alfozan. (U.S. Department of Justice, via Reuters)
inline_images.alt: An image from the Justice Department shows what prosecutors said was an audio recording device hidden in an OpenAI executive conference room by Mr. Alfozan.

news.author: Emmy Martin
news.content_snippet:
A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden recording device at the company captured dozens of internal meetings, including at least one between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government, federal prosecutors said in a court filing on Monday.

The engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, sorted into folders by date and renamed according to their contents, prosecutors said. Many of the recordings involved what appeared to be con
news.summary_en: Federal prosecutors disclosed in court filings that former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan used OpenAI’s Codex AI tool to configure recording devices, capturing dozens of confidential meetings, including sensitive discussions with a foreign government. While data exfiltration remains under investigation, the act constitutes a significant breach of trade secrets and attorney-client privilege.
paragraphs: A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden recording device at the company captured dozens of internal meetings, including at least one between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government, federal prosecutors said in a court filing on Monday.

The engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, sorted into folders by date and renamed according to their contents, prosecutors said. Many of the recordings involved what appeared to be confidential trade secrets, including meetings with OpenAI customers, they said, and OpenAI identified others as containing material protected by attorney-client privilege.

The filing, which opposes Mr. Alfozan’s request to be released from jail before trial, offers the most detailed account yet of what investigators say he recorded. It also comes days after prosecutors told a federal judge that they were “not aware of any” evidence that Mr. Alfozan had committed espionage, stolen trade secrets or acted as an agent of a foreign government.
Prosecutors did not say in Monday’s filing that he had shared the recordings with anyone. “What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation,” they wrote.

Mr. Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and U.S. permanent resident, has been charged with one count of illegally intercepting conversations and has pleaded not guilty. A hearing on his release is scheduled for Tuesday morning.

His lawyer, David Rizk, argued in a filing last week that the case had turned out to be far less serious than prosecutors initially suggested, describing his client as “an overly curious tinkerer.” Mr. Rizk wrote that the vast majority of recordings on Mr. Alfozan’s computer “apparently contain just random noise and silence.”
Mr. Rizk could not be immediately reached for comment on Monday.

According to prosecutors, the recordings span 15 folders dated Sept. 8 to Sept. 28 and include meetings held on 12 days in an executive conference room. One file was titled “1200-sovereign-bilateral-briefing-sep22.” The filing did not identify the foreign government.

Mr. Alfozan used Codex, an OpenAI A.I. tool, through his wife’s account to help configure the recording device, add voice detection so it would “only record speech,” and move recordings through a Dropbox account, prosecutors said. His wife has not been accused of wrongdoing.

Prosecutors also said he photographed each printed page of a confidential term sheet for a “strategic partnership” between OpenAI and another company in the early hours of Oct. 5. That was the same day a hidden camera recorded him checking behind the television where OpenAI’s security team had found the listening device days earlier.

The filing also described Mr. Alfozan’s contact with Saudi officials. On Oct. 6, a member of the Saudi royal family sent him a link to Echelon, a Riyadh-based A.I. company, and asked: “Time to move back to KSA and join us?”

Mr. Alfozan suggested he might do so “after the IPO,” prosecutors said. The night before his Oct. 9 arrest, he spoke with the Saudi official by WhatsApp for 16 minutes. Prosecutors said he had also exchanged WhatsApp messages with officials at Saudi Arabia’s communications ministry, including the minister in August and September.

news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.content_snippet:
French and U.S. authorities suspect Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe, an incident that reportedly spoiled food and caused equipment failures, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in damage. The attack affected about 700 supermarkets, raising concerns about the exposure of connected refrigeration systems and the potential for cyber operations to disrupt essential commercial infrastructure.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot
news.summary_en: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot officially attributed the cyberattack on over 700 European supermarket refrigeration controllers to Iran's 'SHAHID KAVEH' cyber unit during a G7 meeting. The attack, occurring between October 11-12, caused widespread equipment failures, fires, and tens of millions of euros in food losses, marking a transition from espionage to physical infrastructure sabotage.
paragraphs: French and U.S. authorities suspect Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe, an incident that reportedly spoiled food and caused equipment failures, resulting in tens of millions of dollars in damage. The attack affected about 700 supermarkets, raising concerns about the exposure of connected refrigeration systems and the potential for cyber operations to disrupt essential commercial infrastructure.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused Tehran of orchestrating the attack, warning that Iran would face retribution. Speaking Monday at a Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Paris, Barrot described the incident as the first large-scale cyberattack conducted for sabotage on French national territory, calling it a major threat to the country’s interests and the security of its population.

“Following its investigation, France is able to attribute these destructive actions to Iran, carried out by the SHAHID KAVEH cyber offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” France’s Foreign Ministry wrote in a Monday statement attributing cyberattacks targeting France to Iran. “This actor poses a persistent threat to our critical infrastructure.”

It added that these destructive cyberattacks are unjustifiable, inexcusable, and violate international law. “They also contravene the principles of the United Nations’ normative framework for responsible state behavior in cyberspace, to which the Islamic Republic of Iran has subscribed.”

The agency highlighted that the Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024. In March 2026, the European Union adopted sanctions against the Iranian entity Emmenet Pasargad, which had contributed to conducting these cyberattacks.”

During the night of October 11-12, a cyberattack campaign targeted supermarket refrigeration controllers deployed in over 700 major retail locations across France. These cyberattacks caused considerable material damage, fires, and food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.

The agency recognized that “this is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory.”

The incident highlights the potential consequences of cyberattacks against connected systems outside traditional IT networks, particularly refrigeration infrastructure used to preserve food supplies and maintain supermarket operations. Reported damage ranged from spoiled inventory and equipment failures, underscoring how attacks on OT (operational technology) infrastructure can translate into direct economic losses and disruption to services relied on by the public.

“In accordance with the 2026 national cybersecurity strategy, France is determined to use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace,” the agency added. “Consequently, France will summon the Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran to France to express its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks.”

Furthermore, France will propose to its European partners the adoption of new sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved in this cyberattack against it, as well as in other malicious cyber activities.
Finally, France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.
In response, Iran has described French accusations that it was behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers as ‘baseless and hostile.’

paragraphs: Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue climbed 50% year-over-year to $14.5 billion, topping Wall Street estimates of $14.3 billion.HPE projected Q1 revenue outlook between $14 billion to $14.6 billion, marginally lower than the highest Wall Street estimates of $14.7 billion.The cloud infrastructure firm lifted its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to as high as $63.1 billion.Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. (HPE) reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue and profit that surpassed Wall Street expectations on Monday, however, its share price slipped after-hours as its Q1 FY27 outlook fell short of the rosiest of Wall Street expectations.For the quarter ended October 31, the Houston-based technology company posted revenue of $14.5 billion, up 50% from the same period a year earlier and ahead of the $14.3 billion average forecast from analysts polled by Fiscal.ai.

The cloud infrastructure firm reported earnings of $1.43 per share, beating the consensus projection of $1.28 a share. “We are now a fundamentally different company, with greater earnings power, a stronger competitive position, and a portfolio built to capitalize on the next phase of AI,” said Antonio Neri, president and CEO of HPE.

AI Servers And Juniper Integration Drive GrowthHPE’s rapid expansion was anchored by its Cloud & AI division, where quarterly revenue jumped 68.6% year-over-year to $11.3 billion and operating margins nearly doubled to 18.4% from 9.3%. Within that unit, server revenue soared 94.7% to $8.8 billion on the back of demand for systems powered by Nvidia Corp.(NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.(AMD) processors, while storage revenue rose 33.8% to $1.5 billion.

The company’s networking segment, bolstered by its integration of Juniper Networks, generated $3.1 billion in revenue, representing a 12.3% increase over the prior year with an operating profit margin of 22.1%. HPE Fiscal 2027 Earnings GuidanceHPE now projects fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 27% to 35% with revenues reaching as high as $63.1 billion, beating analyst expectations of $55.05 billion.

Full-year adjusted earnings are projected to reach up to $5.35 per share.For the current fiscal first quarter ending in January, HPE forecast revenue between $14 billion and $14.6 billion. While the bottom-line guidance comfortably exceeded Wall Street’s average estimate of $1.08 per share, the top-line range fell just shy of the most bullish analyst projections of $14.7 billion, tempering investor enthusiasm.HPE Stock: Retail View Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘extremely bullish’ with ‘extremely high’ message volumes.

paragraphs: Investing.com -- The European Union and Canada are preparing to outline a broad strategic alliance aimed at deepening economic, defense, and trade ties, according to a report from Bloomberg. The effort reflects an intentional push by middle powers to counter the growing dominance of great-power politics led by the U.S. and China.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is slated to announce the initiative during her annual state of the union address in Strasbourg on Sept. 16. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will attend the speech and is expected to address European lawmakers the following day, underscoring Ottawa's commitment to forging closer integration short of formal EU membership.

The upcoming framework aims to expand cooperation across critical supply chains, raw materials, space exploration, and scientific research. Negotiations are also focused on strengthening joint defense capabilities, building on Ottawa's move last year to become the first non-EU country to participate in the bloc's €150 billion ($174 billion) defense procurement fund.

This diplomatic push follows earlier warnings from Prime Minister Carney, who declared at the World Economic Forum that the traditional rules-based international order has effectively fractured. Against that backdrop, both jurisdictions are seeking structural counterweights to unilateral economic pressure tactics and rising global trade friction.

The alliance builds on an existing bilateral trade agreement and security partnership, with officials exploring how close Canada can legally align with the EU's single market. While discussions remain ongoing regarding necessary regulatory or legal mechanisms, both sides are scheduled to formalize next steps during a joint summit in Canada this October.
EU and Canada plan broad alliance to counter U.S.-China dominance - Bloomberg
